problem: Prior studies of shared control and delegation for blind users of navigation robots used Wizard-of-Oz descriptions, short first-time sessions and simple routes. Little is known about how delegation preferences change with repeated use of a fully autonomous system in real settings.
motivation: Fully autonomous guide robots freeze in crowds or at obstacles, so user-robot collaboration is needed. Blind users also value social autonomy and want to choose when to rely on the robot. Novelty effects mean single-session preferences may not be stable, so a multi-week study in a real museum was needed.
key_idea: Run a three-week repeated-exposure field study with six blind participants using a suitcase guide robot with GPT-based scene and obstacle descriptions and button-based delegation of social requests, to observe how delegation strategies evolve.
insight: Delegation is situational and personality-dependent, and it shifts with experience. Initially independent participants (P1, P5, P6) raised delegation (e.g. P5 20% to 100%, P6 0% to 54.5%) mainly in noisy or crowded settings where the robot's louder voice worked better. Participants also learned to read the robot's small corrective motions as 'searching' rather than stuck, and moved from curiosity-driven to targeted use of the descriptions. Mixed-effects tests showed Week significantly raised preference for robot-mediated asking (p=.0016 and p=.0014) but not confidence (p=.33), so first-encounter preferences are unreliable.
method: Robot platform: open-source CaBot suitcase-style guide robot with LiDAR, three RGB-D cameras, a handle with four buttons and haptic feedback, a phone connected to a neck speaker, and an external speaker.
Surrounding GPT: the top button sends a front RGB-D frame to GPT with the generic prompt 'Please describe this scene.' It returns a broad description of objects, people, layout and scene impression.

Obstacle-specific GPT explanations: when the built-in detector flags person, object or unknown obstacle, a front frame plus a constrained prompt goes to GPT-4o. The one-sentence output gives crowd size, line or crowd, facing direction, or the obstacle type.
Social delegation buttons: the right button makes the robot say 'Excuse me, please move' and the left button 'Excuse me, please help me', so users can delegate or speak themselves.

Study design: six blind participants, three weekly sessions of about 2 hours (about 60 min walking), on museum routes with staged crowds, obstacles (foam block, suitcases, stroller) and lines, plus natural visitor crowds.

Measures: delegation rate (delegated interactions divided by obstacle alerts), Surrounding GPT press counts, action rate after obstacle alerts, RoSAS, five Likert items, linear mixed-effects models, and weekly interviews.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (frozen) for obstacle explanations; GPT (unspecified version) for Surrounding GPT; CaBot autonomous navigation stack
setting.training_data: none (training-free; prompted GPT, existing CaBot navigation)
setting.observation: Front RGB-D camera frames, plus LiDAR and three RGB-D cameras for navigation and obstacle detection
setting.action_space: Autonomous waypoint navigation to a destination; user issues button commands (describe, ask people to move, ask for help)
setting.privileged: Pre-built map and waypoints for the museum routes; actors staged the crowds, lines and obstacles

numbers_note: No navigation benchmark results; this is a human-factors user study. Its results are delegation percentages, usage counts and Likert ratings, which fit no benchmark metric.
results: Delegation to the robot rose over weeks for the initially independent users: P5 went from 20.0% to 100%, P6 from 0.0% to 54.5%, and P1 from 0.0% to 57.1% in Week 2, then 12.5% in Week 3. Week significantly predicted preference for robot asking people to move (F(2,10)=13.57, p=.0016) and for robot asking for help (F(2,10)=13.21, p=.0014), and predicted understanding via descriptions (p=.0071). It did not significantly predict confidence (p=.33) or the RoSAS scores.
limitations: Only six participants, three sessions, one museum, and partly staged scenarios, so generalisation and statistical power are limited
The system could not separate lines from crowds, offered no interactive Q&A for descriptions, and sometimes got stuck on unplanned obstacles such as slanted walls
Robot speech was in a single language, so it often went unnoticed by international visitors
builds_on: Kamikubo et al. 2025 (Beyond Wizard-of-Oz delegation study)
compares_to: Kamikubo et al. 2025 (Wizard-of-Oz shared control study)
